title: Cheaper turns: a fast gate and scripts instead of bookkeeping

C1.rule: Mechanical, one owned file, fully specified, no design choice

C2.rule: Bounded implementation or tests, clear spec, one or two owned files and their tests

C3.rule: Cross-module design; changes a gate or the ledger contract; wrong means every project inherits it

C4.rule: Planning, merging, reconciling, anything in a project's real data, a sponsor decision

items.title: No waiting on a gate: one blocking call, one verdict line
items.what: An agent that backgrounds a gate and polls it spends a full context re-send (~134k tokens, measured) per check to learn nothing. The standard says: run the gate in the foreground, read the verdict line in the same turn, never park a turn on a timer. Mandatory Standard change, in the brief template, the lead prompt and CLAUDE-workflow.md.
items.done: A Standard change (mandatory) CHANGELOG entry; the rule in templates/brief.md, templates/lead-prompt.md and CLAUDE-workflow.md; a test that fails if the brief template loses it.

items.title: bin/commit-if-green: gate, verdict and commit in one call
items.what: Today a builder reads the gate's verdict, then issues git add, git commit and git push as separate tool calls -- four model turns for a mechanical sequence, and the OK/FAILED check is applied by the model rather than by code. One wrapper runs the gate, commits and pushes only on a verdict line matching ^OK with no ^FAILED, and reports what it did.
items.done: Refuses on FAILED, on a non-zero exit and on an empty verdict; commits nothing in either case; tested against a fixture repo with a passing and a failing gate.

log.event: Built bin/commit-if-green: runs the gate through bin/quiet, commits and pushes only when quiet's verdict line starts "quiet: OK" and quiet's own exit code is 0. Refuses before running anything on bad usage, --push to main, a merge/rebase in progress, or nothing to commit; treats FAILED, a nonzero exit, or an empty/unrecognised verdict line as failure -- never as success. tests/test_commit_if_green.py (15 cases) against throwaway repos with a fake gate. Evidence: commit sha pending (recorded after push).
Recorded evidence: commit 3a59e5c on branch o04-commit-if-green.
log.evidence: commit 3a59e5c on branch o04-commit-if-green: bin/commit-if-green + tests/test_commit_if_green.py (16 cases, python3 -m unittest test_commit_if_green test_quiet -q ran green -- narrow set, since affected_tests.py names two dozen modules only because the ledger json changed, not because the tool touches them)

items.what: Six briefs in one message cost one lead turn; six messages cost six. The standard already says to spawn every unblocked C1/C2 item in one message -- say it as a cost rule, with the same rule for reviewing branches, and say that a lead never sends a brief a turn at a time.

items.title: A staging branch, so main is never red
items.what: The sponsor: "We can also reduce the number of tests so we can have a development branch or a staging branch where we can keep merging changes and then after a considerable amount of changes are done, we can test in one go." Reviewed branches merge into staging; the full suite runs there, not on main; main fast-forwards from staging only when staging is green. No test is deleted -- what is reduced is the number of runs, not the coverage (finance-tracker had 1,753 green tests over 16 wrong-money defects).
items.done: bin/land knows the staging target; the standard says where the full suite runs and when main advances; a red staging branch cannot reach main; tested on a fixture repo.

log.event: bin/land learns staging_branch (.common-rules.json): a reviewed branch lands there instead of main, creating it from main on first use, same gate unchanged; main only ever moves through 'land --advance-staging', which re-runs the gate on staging and fast-forwards main on a green verdict only, refusing on red, on staging behind main, or on an unreadable verdict. tools/project.py documents/validates the key. Standard change (mandatory) in CLAUDE-workflow.md's Tests section, pointed to from Git, lead-prompt.md and brief.md. tests/test_land_staging.py, 11 cases. No test deleted; no project declares it yet.
Recorded evidence: commit a54eccb on branch o08-staging-branch.

items.title: Warm-up stops shelling out 23 times to measure conformance
items.what: Finding 31/F-01: bin/warmup costs 1.9s, of which 1.21s is bin/conformance measure running 23 subprocesses. Every session pays it at startup and test_warmup pays it 122 times. The 23 checks are independent reads -- import them in-process, or run them concurrently, or both. Same verdicts, same output, faster.
items.done: bin/warmup's wall clock measured before and after on the same commit; conformance reports identical verdicts for the same repo state; the 12-check suite stays green.

log.event: Item 12 and item 7 now call bin/warmup and bin/proposalcheck in process instead of as subprocesses; the 12 checks run concurrently in a thread pool, order preserved. Byte identical output proven before and after. Measured on the same loaded machine, load average about 5.7 to 8.2, three runs each, same commit: bin/warmup 3.7 to 4.2 seconds down to 2.1 seconds; bin/conformance 3.7 seconds down to 2.1 seconds. Subprocess spawns 47 git plus 2 python interpreters down to 62 git plus 0 python interpreters, the 15 extra git calls were always made, just previously hidden inside the two eliminated child processes (measured in isolation: warmup --check alone makes 13, proposalcheck alone makes 2). run_inprocess catches exceptions and reports a crash as a failed check rather than propagating through the thread pool. Gate: test_conformance plus test_rulecheck, 150 tests in 115.080 seconds, OK. test_warmup's own before/after is O-02's to measure on a quiet machine, in its own worktree.

items.title: Shards split within a file, not just between files
items.what: Finding 31/F-02: bin/quiet shards by test file, so the suite's floor is its slowest file however many cores are free -- which is why --jobs 8 measured 610s. Shard by test class (or by an even split of test ids) so one 575s file spreads across cores.
items.done: The slowest file's tests run across several processes; aggregated counts still match a sequential run; --jobs 8 measured against serial on the same commit.

log.event: Sharding now splits within a file: a Unit is a file or a group of its test classes, planned against the balanced target from the duration cache. 38 test_quiet tests green. The real-suite measurement is deliberately left to O-02, on a quiet machine.

items.title: ruflo-item records several items in one invocation
items.what: Finding 31/F-05: every call stops the daemon in a finally (rightly -- it spawns headless sessions that burn tokens), so the next call cold-starts it. One call is 3.3s; ten items back to back did not finish in 500s. Accept several ids in one invocation -- and a --from-ledger mode that records every item closed since a date -- starting the daemon once and stopping it once.
items.done: Several ids recorded in one invocation with one daemon start and one stop, measured against the same ids one at a time; the daemon is still stopped in a finally on every exit path, including a crash; tested on a fixture.

log.event: start/done accept repeatable --item ID:TEXT to batch several ids in one invocation (one binary resolution, one daemon start/stop); new from-ledger LEDGER [--since DATE] backfills item:<ID>:start/done from a ledger's done items without re-running the gate. Measured on a scratch repo, real binary: baseline 4 single calls for 2 items = 11.4s; batched start+done for the same 2 ids = 8.6s; from-ledger for 2 items = 3.3s. Gate: tests/test_ruflo_item.py + test_ruflo + test_conformance, 163 tests, OK.

items.title: workflow.html's stamp is generated, not hand-typed
items.what: docs/README.md's rule is that any PR changing the shared rules updates docs/workflow.html and its version stamp in the same PR. Three merges on 17 Sep did not, main went red on test_workflow_stamp, and the lead then hand-stamped the page twice in one evening because each rules merge bumps the number it must match. A script writes the stamp from git and regenerates the png, so the only hand-written part is the prose describing the new rule.

log.evidence: No contradiction after all: CLAUDE.md line 18 governs INITIATIVE -- a session never starts a rules change of its own accord -- while the 14 Sep ruling governs MECHANICS: a change the sponsor directed, once its gate is green and review has passed, is merged by the lead rather than handed back as a gh command. bin/land keeps refusing to auto-land inside common-rules, for the reason written beside that guard: landing automatically would let the AI change the rules it operates under without anyone saying yes. findings.title: Every ruflo-item call stops the daemon in a finally, so the next one cold-starts it: a single call is 3.3s but ten items back to back did not finish in 500s. There is no way to record several items in one invocation, so a lead closing a batch pays the cold start every time

log.event: catalogued
corrected
log.evidence: My premise was wrong. I wrote this finding claiming the daemon's cold start dominates, from a backfill where ten items recorded two in 500s. O-11's careful measurement at load 4-5 says a single call is ~3.3s (start) and ~2.5s (done), so four calls are 11.4s, not 250s each. The 500s backfill was machine contention -- three test suites were running -- not daemon churn. What O-11 actually buys, measured: batching two items 11.4s -> 8.6s (25%), and `from-ledger` 11.4s -> 3.3s (3.4x) because it skips the gate and the hooks. The ergonomic win stands -- one call instead of twenty for a backfill -- but the cold-start rationale in this finding's title does not.
